title: Linear Algebra
body:
Linear Algebra studies [[System of Linear Equations|linear systems]] and the objects that solve
them: [[Vector|vectors]], [[Matrix|matrices]] and the
[[Linear Transformation|transformations]] matrices represent. Linear means every unknown
appears to the first power and never multiplied by another unknown, which rules out squares,
products of variables and trigonometric terms.

That restriction looks severe and it buys something large. Linear problems are solvable
mechanically, in polynomial time, in any number of dimensions, by one algorithm that never
needs cleverness. Almost every computationally tractable problem is either linear or is being
approximated by something linear.

For this degree it is the most reused mathematics in the building. A [[Forward Pass]] through a
neural network is [[Matrix Multiplication]], a neuron's weighted sum is a [[Dot Product]], and
dimensionality reduction is [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] of a covariance matrix.
[[MACHINE LEARNING]] reaches this note by a shorter path than any other math course.

One idea holds the rest together: choosing the right [[Basis]] converts a hard problem into an
easy one. [[Diagonalization]] is that idea with the details filled in.

## Topics

### Solving a system

A [[System of Linear Equations]] has no solutions, exactly one, or infinitely many. Two
distinct solutions are impossible, because any two solutions generate a whole line of them,
which is a geometric fact about intersecting flat objects.

[[Gaussian Elimination]] is the algorithm that decides which case holds and produces the
answer. It uses three row operations: swapping two rows, scaling a row by a non-zero constant,
and adding a multiple of one row to another. Each preserves the solution set, which is what
makes the method legal.

$$
\begin{cases} x + 2y = 5 \\ 3x - y = 1 \end{cases}
\qquad
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]
$$

```
R2 - 3R1:   [ 1   2 |  5 ]        eliminate x from the second row
            [ 0  -7 | -14]

R2 / -7:    [ 1   2 |  5 ]        y = 2
            [ 0   1 |  2 ]

R1 - 2R2:   [ 1   0 |  1 ]        x = 1
            [ 0   1 |  2 ]
```

The augmented matrix carries the coefficients and the right-hand side, and the operations act
on rows, so the variable names are never written again. In echelon form an inconsistent system
shows a row reading $0 = c$ for a non-zero $c$, and a column with no leading entry gives a
free variable, meaning infinitely many solutions with one parameter each. The algorithm costs
$O(n^3)$, and it also inverts matrices, computes determinants and extracts bases, which makes
it the computational core of the course.

[[Matrix Inverse]] covers what plays the role of division. [[Cramer's Rule]] gives a closed
form for the solution and demonstrates that a closed form and a good algorithm are separate
things, since it costs far more than elimination on anything larger than a small system.

### Matrices

[[Matrix]] covers notation, addition, scalar multiplication, the transpose and the special
shapes. [[Matrix Multiplication]] follows the row-by-column rule because it is function
composition, so the inner dimensions have to match:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The entry in row $i$ and column $j$ of the product is the [[Dot Product]] of row $i$ of the
first matrix with column $j$ of the second. The two products above differ, which is the
concrete meaning of [[Non-Commutative]]: the second matrix swaps columns on the right and
swaps rows on the left, and those are different operations. A product $AB$ reads right to
left, with the rightmost matrix acting first, matching the notation $f(g(x))$.

Three more differences from scalar algebra. The order reverses under transpose and inverse,
giving $(AB)^T = B^TA^T$ and $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$, because undoing two operations means
undoing the last one first. A product $AB = 0$ permits both factors to be non-zero. And
$AB = AC$ permits $B \neq C$, so cancellation is unavailable.

This vault writes vectors as columns with matrices applied on the left, as $A\mathbf{x}$.
Machine learning code frequently stores samples as rows and writes $\mathbf{x}A$, which
transposes every formula in these notes.

### Determinants

The [[Determinant]] is one number recording how much a matrix scales area or volume, with its
sign recording whether orientation flips. For a $2 \times 2$ matrix it is $ad - bc$, so
$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $-2$, meaning it doubles area
and reflects.

A determinant of zero means the transformation collapsed a dimension, flattening the plane
onto a line, and a collapsed dimension cannot be recovered, which is why zero determinant and
non-invertible are the same condition. The note covers cofactor expansion, evaluation by row
reduction, and the multiplicative property $\det(AB) = \det A \det B$, alongside
$\det(A^T) = \det A$ and $\det(A^{-1}) = 1/\det A$.

Cofactor expansion costs $O(n!)$ and row reduction costs $O(n^3)$. Both compute the same
number, and at $n = 20$ only one of them finishes.

For a square matrix a long list of conditions all say the same thing: the determinant is
non-zero, the matrix is invertible, its columns are independent, its columns form a basis, its
kernel is trivial, its rank is $n$, it row-reduces to $I$, and $0$ is not among its
eigenvalues. [[Matrix Inverse]] holds the full table, and the value of it is that a question
about any one condition can be answered by checking whichever is easiest.

### Vectors and vector spaces

A [[Vector]] is an ordered list of $n$ numbers. The [[Dot Product]] multiplies two vectors
into a single number and satisfies
$\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta$, so a dot product of zero
means the vectors are perpendicular. That is how perpendicularity extends to $\mathbb{R}^n$
and to spaces of functions, where no picture is available, and it is where projection comes
from.

[[Vector Space]] gives the ten axioms and the definition of a subspace, which has to contain
$\mathbf{0}$ and stay closed under both operations, so a line missing the origin fails to
qualify. Matrices, polynomials, functions and solution sets of linear differential equations
all satisfy the axioms, which is what makes the abstraction worth stating: a theorem proved
once holds for all of them.

[[Linear Dependence]] tests a set for redundancy, where a set is dependent when one member is
a combination of the others. Independence and spanning are separate conditions, and a
[[Basis]] satisfies both at once, which is the exact point where reaching everything meets
carrying no redundancy. Every basis of a space has the same size, and that number is the
dimension, so more than $n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are always dependent. Coordinates depend
on the choice of basis while the vector itself does not. In an orthonormal basis coordinates
come from one dot product each and no system needs solving, which is the mechanism
[[Fourier Series]] runs on.

### Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

[[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] finds the directions a matrix leaves pointing the same way,
stretching them without rotating them:

$$
A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}
$$

Worked on $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. The eigenvalues come from the
characteristic equation:

$$
\det(A - \lambda I) = (2-\lambda)^2 - 1 = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = 0
\;\Rightarrow\; \lambda = 3, \; 1
$$

Solving $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for each gives
$\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ for $\lambda = 3$ and
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$ for $\lambda = 1$. Checking the first:
$A\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = 3\mathbf{v}_1$, so the direction is
unchanged and the length triples.

The eigenvalues sum to the trace, $3 + 1 = 4$, and multiply to the determinant,
$3 \times 1 = 3$, which is a free check on the arithmetic and worth performing every time.
Only square matrices have eigenvalues, complex eigenvalues indicate a rotation with no
real direction left fixed, and $\lambda = 0$ indicates a singular matrix.

[[Diagonalization]] writes $A = PDP^{-1}$, where $P$ holds the eigenvectors as columns and $D$
holds the eigenvalues on the diagonal, which is possible when $A$ has $n$ independent
eigenvectors. Symmetric matrices always qualify, with real eigenvalues and orthogonal
eigenvectors. The payoff is that powers collapse:

$$
A^k = PD^kP^{-1}
$$

since the $P^{-1}P$ pairs cancel in the middle, and raising a diagonal matrix to a power means
raising each diagonal entry. A hundredth power of a matrix becomes a hundredth power of two
numbers. The same move decouples a system of [[Differential Equations]] into independent
scalar equations, which is what [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] does with it.

### Linear transformations

A [[Linear Transformation]] respects linear combinations, satisfying
$T(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u})+T(\mathbf{v})$ and $T(c\mathbf{u}) = cT(\mathbf{u})$,
which forces $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$. That is why $f(x) = mx + b$ with $b \neq 0$ falls
outside the definition despite being called a linear function in high school.

The standard matrix of $T$ is built by applying $T$ to each basis vector and using the results
as columns, since a linear map is determined entirely by what it does to a basis. Rotation by
90 degrees sends $\mathbf{e}_1 = (1,0)$ to $(0,1)$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 = (0,1)$ to $(-1,0)$,
giving $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$. The geometric operators are rotation,
reflection, shear and projection.

[[Kernel and Range]] records what a map destroys and what it can reach. The range is the
column space and the kernel is the solution set of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$. Rank plus
nullity equals the number of columns, and a trivial kernel is equivalent to the map being
one-to-one, since a linear map that collapses two inputs together collapses their difference
to zero.

### Complex numbers

[[Complex Numbers]] introduces $i^2 = -1$ along with arithmetic, conjugates, and division by
multiplying through by the conjugate of the denominator. They enter a linear algebra course
for a specific reason: a rotation matrix has no real eigenvector, because no real direction
survives a rotation unchanged, and its characteristic equation has complex roots. In
$\mathbb{C}$ every degree-$n$ polynomial has exactly $n$ roots, and the complex roots of a
real polynomial arrive in conjugate pairs.

[[Polar Form]] writes a complex number by modulus and argument, where multiplication
multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments, so multiplying by $z$ rotates by $\arg z$ and
scales by $|z|$. De Moivre's theorem, the roots of unity, and Euler's formula
$e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ are all restatements of that one fact.

## Related courses

- [[DISCRETE MATH]] supplies [[Sets]] for the notation underneath
  [[Vector Space]] and [[Proof By Induction]] for the arguments about dimension.
- [[CALCULUS 1]] and [[CALCULUS 2]] supply the [[Trigonometric Function]] identities that
  [[Polar Form]] runs on.
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] makes the same axiomatic move a second time, since a
  [[Group]] and a [[Vector Space]] are both sets with operations and axioms. It also treats
  [[Complex Numbers]] as a field extension.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] is the direct sequel and the destination for
  most of this course. The chain runs [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]], the
  [[Spectral Theorem]], the [[Singular Value Decomposition]] and
  [[Principal Component Analysis]], which is the vault's route from the math block into
  [[MACHINE LEARNING]]. [[Least Squares]] replaces
  [[Matrix Inverse|$A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$]] when the system has no solution, [[Projection]]
  derives it, [[Vector Norm]] is where loss functions come from, and [[Pseudoinverse]] handles
  the matrices this course leaves out.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] covers vectors that vary from point to point in
  [[Vector Calculus]], through the [[Gradient]], [[Curl]] and [[Divergence]], and picks up the
  eigenvalue application where $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ decouples in the eigenvector basis.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] takes [[Complex Numbers]] and [[Polar Form]] as
  prerequisites, and treats [[Fourier Series]] as an [[Orthogonal Functions|orthonormal basis]]
  expansion in an infinite-dimensional space of functions.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] use [[Forward Pass]] as matrix
  multiplication, a neuron as a [[Dot Product]] against its [[Weights]] followed by an
  [[Activation Function]], and [[Back Propagation]] as the chain rule over that structure.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] analyses [[Gaussian Elimination]] and naive
  [[Matrix Multiplication]], both $O(n^3)$, and the $O(n!)$ against $O(n^3)$ gap for
  determinants is the clearest argument in the vault for measuring [[Time Complexity]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] and [[Leetcode]] store a [[Matrix]] as a
  two-dimensional [[Array]], and [[Matrix Traversal]] reads the same storage as a [[Graph]].
- [[CLASSICAL PHYSICS 1]] uses the [[Vector]] on every force and velocity, and
  [[Vector Components]] is the resolution that turns a two-dimensional problem into two
  one-dimensional ones.
